newsitem.title: USA: N.Carolina may finally give governor veto.
newsitem.headline: N.Carolina may finally give governor veto.

text.p: Voters in North Carolina will choose national and state representatives on Election Day and will also decide whether to amend the state constitution to give the governor veto power.
North Carolina is the only U.S. state that does not grant its governor the power to veto legislation and Tuesday will be the first time the amendment has appeared on a state ballot.
"This is really a fight over power: legislative versus gubernatorial," said Thad Beyle, political science professor at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill.
It is a power struggle begun after the Revolutionary War by legislators who retaliated against colonial governors.

"The state had a history of very bad colonial governors early in its history, bad Reconstruction (post-Civil War) governors, and we were the first state to impeach its governor," said Ran Coble, executive director of the North Carolina Centre for Public Policy Research Inc.
Without veto power, a legislature controlled by one party could stay the hand of a governor from the other party.

Gov. Jim Hunt, who will steer the state into the next millennium if re-elected, is a Democrat. But the state House of Representatives was taken over by Republicans for the first time in a century in the 1994 election, while the Senate narrowly remained Democratic.

Political analysts said the amendment comes now because Republicans, heady with power after the sweeping change in the 1994 national elections that installed a Republican-led Congress, called for it in a state-level Republican "contract" that included veto power for the governor.

"After the '94 debacle for the Democrats ... the Republicans may have thought that since they captured the House and almost the Senate there was some wave for a Republican governor," said Abraham Holtzman of North Carolina State University, who is opposed to the amendment.

Opponents argue veto power would increase conflict and bitterness between the governor and the legislature and reduce the need for the governor to rely on persuasion and logic in dealing with the legislature.

Aside from balancing power between executive and legislative branches, proponents argue veto power could also serve as a check against the passage of legislation rushed through the General Assembly without full deliberation or not in the public interest.
Hunt, 59, a three-term incumbent, is being challenged by Republican Robin Hayes, 51, a textile mill-owner and the grandson of textiles magnate Charlie Cannon.
